t: How To Teach At A Rewards-Focused School
q: A do-this-and-get-that approach to classroom management is damaging to kids. It snuffs out intrinsic motivation and turns the student-teacher relationship into a cold-hearted transaction.
The key is to offer them to your students without connecting them to any particular behavior.
If you're required to hand out external rewards, then joyfully give them to everyone in your class at the same time.
Just pass them out at odd times without explanation, even to the student sitting in time-out. It is, after all, a free gift with no strings attached.
Free grace has a remarkable way of softening hearts and reawakening intrinsic motivational engines. It’s also a model for what true giving looks like.
Simple and consistent kindness, pleasantness, and friendliness, without expectation of receiving anything in return, is a core principle here at SCM.
x: Teachers can stay true to their values around intrinsic motivation even while complying with a school's rewards mandate.

Linsin acknowledges his well-known opposition to exchanging rewards for expected behavior, but pivots here to offer practical guidance for teachers whose schools mandate token systems like tickets or stickers.
The three principles are give to everyone, give for fun, and give as a lesson in unconditional generosity.
Giving rewards to every student at the same time, for no stated reason, avoids the transactional dynamic of behavior-based rewards.
Unconditional giving models grace and reinforces that learning and belonging are rewards in themselves.

t: How To Improve Classroom Management Every Day very-day/
q: One of the secrets to exceptional classroom management is to aim for the stars.
But you mustn’t settle for just okay. You mustn’t merely hope to keep a lid on your classroom.
The way it works is that you’re going to keep a short daily list of the routines, behaviors, and activities that were done perfectly as well as a list of the areas that need work.
You won’t add a lecture. You won’t threaten or feign disappointment. You won’t over-praise, raise your voice, or give anything but the unvarnished truth.

Feedback, in the form of letting students know directly and honestly how they’re doing, and if what they’re doing is, indeed, how you taught them, is a little-known key to effective classroom management.
It moves your class closer and closer to your dream destination—until the bottom list all but disappears.
There is deep pride in doing things well, in seeing evidence of progress, in getting better every day through the pursuit of excellence.
x: Effective classroom management requires actively pushing for daily improvement, not merely maintaining acceptable behavior.

t: How To Improve Listening With Strategic Pausing https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/01/14/how-to-improve-listening-with-strategic-pausing/
q: Do you ever get the feeling your students aren’t hearing a word you say?
One common denominator among those who struggle with getting students to listen is that they talk too fast.
Pausing, in fact, is one of the most important skills for capturing and keeping attention. It can also improve behavior, eliminate boredom, and make your instruction more interesting.
It breaks up the rhythm of your speech, which can quickly grow monotonous. It brings students back into the fold whose minds have started to wander.
It gives students a chance to download the information, reflect on it, and consider how it pertains to them.
A lengthy pause also adds drama and intrigue to even the most mundane topics. It's a critical element of effective storytelling and can help make your subject come alive for your students.
Instead of slouching down and away in their seats, they’ll lean toward you. Like a field of daisies reaching for the sun.
x: Linsin addresses the common frustration of feeling like students aren't truly listening, tracing much of the problem to teachers speaking too quickly without realizing it.
Many teachers who struggle to hold attention are unknowingly talking too fast, stringing sentences together without breaks.
The piece frames pausing as a foundational storytelling and instructional skill that makes teachers more interesting, their words more meaningful, and their classrooms more attentive.
Pausing mid-sentence breaks up monotonous rhythm and pulls back students whose attention has started to wander.
Longer, even awkward pauses after key points let students process information and anticipate what comes next.

t: Why You Should Pretend Your Most Difficult Students Are Perfectly Well Behaved students-are-perfectly-well-behaved/
q: One of the biggest reasons difficult students misbehave is because they’re often treated with the expectation that they will.
You reinforce the conclusion that they've naturally drawn about themselves that 'behavior problem' is who they are—as much a part of them as their name or eye color.
Labeling has a profound influence on behavior. Yet, a majority of teachers are unaware they're doing it or that it's the primary reason behavior hasn't changed.
If you make a point of pretending that your most challenging students are among the better behaved in the class, then those erroneous beliefs they've been saddled with will start falling away.
When you treat them like everyone else, they begin to feel like a valued member of the class. They begin fulfilling the new prophecy you convey to them through your behavior, words, and actions.
What’s cool about this strategy is that you’ll see a difference within the first day.
Not short-lived improvement, mind you, but change to who they are on the inside. Change that is real, intrinsic, and enduring.
x: Treating difficult students differently — hovering, frequent reminders, modulated tone — functions as a form of labeling that reinforces misbehavior.

Linsin argues that much of difficult students' misbehavior is reinforced by the way teachers treat them differently — hovering nearby, pulling them aside for reminders, or modulating voice and body language around them…
Unconscious behaviors like glaring and hovering are harder to stop precisely because teachers often don't realize they're doing them.

His recommended strategy is to deliberately treat the most challenging students as though they were among the best behaved in the class — smiling, joking, and making eye contact just as with well-behaved students …
